_comment: Water estimates in milliliters per token. Two scopes: conservative (scope-1 on-site cooling water, as companies report it) and academic (full lifecycle, adding the scope-2 water consumed generating the electricity). Update as new research emerges.
_date_fields_note: _last_updated is when this FILE last changed, which is usually just adding a tier for a newly-priced model. _tiers_last_sourced is when the underlying ml-per-token figures were last checked against primary research — a different and much slower-moving thing. These were one field until 2026-08-24, which let routine model additions make the intensity estimates look freshly verified when they had not been re-read since Dec 2025.
_tiers_last_sourced_note: 2026-08-28 re-source, the first since 2025-12. THE ANCHORS DID NOT MOVE. Google's 0.26 ml per median Gemini Apps text prompt and Altman's 0.32 ml per ChatGPT query are still the only first-party per-prompt water figures that exist, and no provider has published a per-TOKEN figure at all. Checked against primary sources rather than coverage: the Google paper (arXiv:2508.15734) is still v1, 21 Aug 2025, never revised; Google's 2026 Environmental Report repeats the same May-2025 measurement unchanged (independently confirmed by this repo's own direct read, transparency-index.json, 2026-08-25); Anthropic still publishes no per-query water figure; Li et al. has since been peer-reviewed but its numbers are unchanged. So the nine-month-old date was stale bookkeeping, not stale evidence. What the pass DID find was six errors in how this file described its own numbers — each is corrected below and flagged inline where it lived. A SECOND pass the same day researched the two _open_questions and found real evidence on both: see _open_questions, which now records that the constant-ml-per-token model is structurally wrong rather than merely mis-calibrated.
_sources: Li, Yang, Islam, Ren — 'Making AI Less Thirsty: Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models' — arXiv:2304.03271 — arxiv.org/abs/2304.03271

Li et al. — peer-reviewed version of the above: Communications of the ACM 68(7):54-63, July 2025 — doi.org/10.1145/3724499 — cite this one wherever a reviewed source matters (added 2026-08-28; we had only ever cited the preprint)
Elsworth et al. (Google) — 'Measuring the environmental impact of delivering AI at Google Scale' — arXiv:2508.15734v1, 21 Aug 2025 — the 0.26 ml anchor and its measurement boundary
Google Cloud blog — 'Measuring the environmental impact of AI inference', Aug 2025 — the public-facing version of the above
Google 2026 Environmental Report — re-read 2026-08-25: per-prompt figures unchanged from May 2025
Sam Altman — 'The Gentle Singularity', Jun 2025 — 0.000085 gallons (= 0.32 ml) per ChatGPT query; a blog statement with no published methodology

Jegham et al. — 'How Hungry is AI? Benchmarking Energy, Water and Carbon Footprint of LLM Inference' — arXiv:2505.09598, May 2025 — per-query energy for 30 models at three KNOWN token configs, plus a water equation matching our conservative/academic split. Load-bearing as of 2026-08-28: this is the benchmark _open_questions is measured against

OpenRouter / 'State of AI: An Empirical 100 Trillion Token Study' — arXiv:2601.10088, 2026 — average prompt+completion tokens per request, the same quantity the extension multiplies. Router/API traffic, so a proxy for chat usage rather than a measurement of it

de Vries-Gao — 'The carbon and water footprints of data centers and what this could mean for artificial intelligence' — Patterns 7(1) 101430, online 17 Dec 2025 — doi.org/10.1016/j.patter.2025.101430 — industry aggregate, not a per-token source
IEEE Spectrum — 'The Real Story on AI Water Usage at Data Centers', Sep 2025 — relays the Li et al. 16.9 ml breakdown
_sources_removed: 2026-08-28: dropped 'moduledge.com AI Water Usage Per-Query Cost analysis - Apr 2026'. ModulEdge s.r.o. sells modular data centres and waterless/liquid cooling — a vendor with a direct commercial interest in this number — and the post only relays Li et al. anyway. It carried the newest date in the list, so it read as our most current evidence while being marketing. We grade providers on the quality of what they disclose; the same bar has to apply to what we cite.
_methodology: CONSERVATIVE SCOPE = scope-1 on-site cooling water only, as companies report it. Anchor: Google's 0.26 ml per median Gemini Apps text prompt (arXiv:2508.15734, measured May 2025). Google's boundary is explicit — 'the water consumed for cooling machines and associated infrastructure in data centers' — computed as (total energy/prompt minus data-centre overhead) x WUE, with WUE 1.15 L/kWh. It EXCLUDES water consumed off-site generating the electricity. Derivation: 0.26 ml / 500 tokens = 0.00052 ml/token for the large tier. That reproduces; the 500-token divisor is our assumption, not Google's (see _open_questions.token_divisor). ACADEMIC SCOPE = full lifecycle, adding the scope-2 water consumed generating the electricity. Reference point: Li et al.'s 16.9 ml per 150-300 word GPT-3 output in an average US data centre (2.2 ml on-site + 14.7 ml electricity). Our 0.020 ml/token large tier is NOT that figure divided by 500 — that would be 0.0338. It is a judgement, and this is the bracket it sits in: Li et al. applied unadjusted gives 0.0338; discounting by the full like-for-like on-site efficiency gain since 2023 (2.2 ml GPT-3 vs 0.26 ml Gemini = 8.5x) gives 0.004. We sit at 0.020, nearer the cautious end, because the electricity-generation share — 87% of the 16.9 ml — tracks grid water intensity, which has not improved 8.5x, while the on-site share has. That reasoning is ours and nobody has measured it. TIERS: scaled by compute intensity, large=100%, medium=65%, small=40%, tiny=25% — also a judgement, not a measurement.

_notes.gemini_official: Google disclosed 0.26 ml per median Gemini Apps text prompt (measured May 2025, published Aug 2025). SCOPE-1 on-site cooling water only — NOT 'scope 1+2'. This file carried the wrong label until 2026-08-28; it implied Google's number already covered electricity-generation water, when that is precisely the gap the academic scope exists to fill, and it was wrong in the direction that flatters the provider. Google's own narrower 'existing approach' methodology gives 0.15 ml for the same prompt. Anchor for the conservative large tier.
_notes.chatgpt_official: Sam Altman stated 0.000085 gallons — 0.32 ml — per average ChatGPT query in 'The Gentle Singularity', Jun 2025. Scope-1 by implication. It is a blog sentence with no published methodology, no stated measurement boundary and no way to audit it; we cite it because it is the only OpenAI figure in existence, not because it is verified. Its closeness to Google's 0.26 ml is reassuring but is not independent confirmation — different scopes, different fleets, one of them unmeasured.
_notes.claude_official: Anthropic has published no per-query or per-model water figure as of 2026-08-28 (re-checked this pass). No environmental report with model-level metrics exists. Claude's tiers here are inferred from comparable frontier models, and that inference is ours.
_notes.academic_range: Li et al.: GPT-3 consumes a 500 ml bottle 'for roughly 10 - 50 medium-length responses, depending on when and where it is deployed' — i.e. 10-50 ml per response, scope 1+2. This file said '~500ml per 20-50 queries = ~10-25ml per query' until 2026-08-28, which halved the top of the authors' own range. IEEE Spectrum's 16.9 ml per 150-300 word output (2.2 on-site + 14.7 electricity) is the same work stated per output. Li et al. describe their own inference estimate as 'on the conservative side'.
_notes.uncertainty: Water intensity varies with data-centre location, cooling method, season and grid fuel mix. Li et al.'s own stated spread is about 5x — the 10-50 responses per bottle above. This file previously claimed variation of '10-25x by location'; that figure was unsourced and appears to be the 10-25 ml-per-query number restated as a multiplier, so it was removed 2026-08-28. Closed-loop liquid cooling cuts direct water use sharply but shifts the burden to electricity, which the conservative scope does not count. These are order-of-magnitude estimates only.
_notes.efficiency_trend: Per-prompt water has fallen sharply. Like-for-like on the on-site scope: GPT-3 in 2023 at 2.2 ml per medium response (Li et al.) against Gemini at 0.26 ml in May 2025 (Google) — about 8.5x. This file previously claimed models are '10-33x more water-efficient per output token'; Google's 33x is its ENERGY reduction over twelve months and the 44x is CARBON — neither is a water figure, and this repo's own transparency-index.json already labels them correctly. Corrected 2026-08-28. Total data-centre water consumption keeps rising with scale regardless of per-prompt gains; Li et al. make the same point.

_open_questions._status: 2026-08-28, second pass the same day: both questions researched further. There IS evidence on both, and it points at something larger than either — the constant-ml-per-token model is structurally wrong, not merely mis-calibrated. Numbers deliberately NOT changed; this is a design decision, not a data refresh.
_open_questions.token_divisor: Evidence now runs against 500. (a) Li et al.'s own 'medium-sized request' — the thing the 16.9 ml figure describes — is ~800 words of input plus 150-300 words of output, i.e. roughly 1,300 tokens. Our academic anchor was divided by a number about 2.6x too small. (b) Google publishes NO token count for its median Gemini prompt (searched the paper directly), so the conservative divisor remains genuinely unsourceable. (c) OpenRouter's 100-trillion-token study (arXiv:2601.10088) measures exactly what the extension multiplies — prompt+completion tokens per request — at over 5,400 by late 2025, up from under 2,000 in late 2023. Caveat: router/API traffic, skewed toward developer and agentic workloads, so a proxy for chat-platform usage rather than a measurement of it.
_open_questions.academic_tier_value: Jegham et al. (arXiv:2505.09598) answers this directly, and we were already citing it without using it. It gives per-query energy for 30 models at three KNOWN token configs (100+300, 1k+1k, 10k+1.5k) and a water equation — Water = E x PUE x WUE_site + E x WUE_source — that is precisely our conservative/academic split. Reconstructing water from its Table 4 energies and Table 1 multipliers reproduces four figures the paper states in prose (219 mL vs 'over 200', 34.7 vs 'only 34', 2.4 and 3.9 vs 'under 4'), so the reconstruction holds. Measured against it, our shipped tiers are roughly right for SHORT queries and overestimate progressively as queries lengthen: full-scope, about 1-2x over at 400 tokens, 1.5-4.6x at 2,000, and 4-15x at 11,500.
_open_questions.the_real_problem: Per-token water is not a constant. In Jegham's data a 28x rise in tokens (400 -> 11,500) raises energy only about 5x, because latency-to-first-token, prefill and idle capacity do not scale with length. A single ml-per-token figure cannot represent a sublinear curve — it can be correct at one query size and nowhere else, so choosing a better divisor only moves where it is right. This is the same direction and shape as the prompt-caching bias already disclosed in sidepanel.html ('we overestimate, and the gap widens as a chat gets longer'), arising from an independent cause, and it is currently undisclosed.
_open_questions.the_40x_multiplier: The scope-1 to full-scope multiplier we ship is 38x (0.020/0.00052), rounded to ~40x in the UI. Real infrastructure implies much less: Google 5.0x (its measured 0.26 mL on-site plus 0.24 Wh x 4.35 L/kWh off-site), Azure/OpenAI 13.9x, AWS/Anthropic 25.9x. It is also not a constant — the BETTER a provider's on-site cooling, the HIGHER its multiplier, because scope-2 stays put while scope-1 shrinks. A single global multiplier is wrong in kind, not only in value.
_open_questions.options: Left open because all three change user-facing numbers. (1) Keep the linear model and re-centre the divisor on a defensible query size — cheapest, still wrong at both ends. (2) Make water a function of query size, the way the cost model already handles context replay — most accurate, most work. (3) Keep the numbers and disclose the bias, as the caching disclaimer already does. Rory's call.
